title: Adaptive toe biomechanical mechanisms underlying obstacle-crossing take-off of jerboas on sand and hard ground
content:
Abstract
Jerboas are typical desert bipedal rodents, whose toes are the only structures that directly contact loose sand during locomotion. The aim of this study was to investigate the toe joint dynamics and biomechanical adaptations that enable jerboas to perform take-off on granular substrates. Using high-speed motion capture and a three-dimensional force-measurement system, we quantified the kinematic and dynamic characteristics of jerboas crossing obstacles of different heights (3–12 cm) on sand and hard ground. The results showed that substrate properties substantially altered the take-off strategy. On hard ground, jerboas relied on efficient force transmission from the substrate to generate propulsion. In contrast, on sand, jerboas showed phase-dependent changes in the angle between the proximal phalanges of the second and third toes and maintained a relatively stable trajectory of the relative angle between adjacent metatarsal segments during the main force-transmission period. These coordinated distal-foot adjustments might help to maintain take-off performance when ground reaction force transmission is reduced and more variable on the granular substrate. These findings reveal a biomechanical mechanism by which jerboas regulate toe joint motion to modulate foot–substrate interaction on yielding terrain. The study also demonstrates how jerboas adjust their take-off strategy in response to different substrates and obstacle heights, providing biomechanical evidence for environmental adaptation in small desert mammals.
